title: Triangle Multiplication is All You Need for Biomolecular Structure Representations
one_liner: Strip out expensive triangle attention from protein-folding models, replace it with simple pair mixing, and run 4x faster while keeping the same accuracy.
lead: AlphaFold-style models predict how proteins fold by reasoning about relationships between every pair of amino acids. But they use a computationally expensive operation called triangle attention (the model tries to understand each pair by looking at all other pairs, repeatedly, which is very slow). Pairmixer replaces this expensive step with a direct blend of pair signals (a fast row-column mixing operation), preserving the model's ability to understand 3D shape while cutting runtime in half and training cost by a third.

problem.h2: Protein folding is slow when it needs to run at scale
paras: AlphaFold-style models predict 3D protein structures by building up a representation of how each pair of amino acids relates to each other. They start with simple guesses about relationships, then refine these guesses by asking: for each pair, how does it connect through all the other pairs? This is a form of attention (the model looks at many things and decides which matter most).

The problem: triangle attention requires many expensive lookups (one for each amino acid, for each layer, for each refinement pass). On a protein with 1000 amino acids running through 48 layers, this is thousands of separate comparisons. For large-scale applications—folding entire protein complexes, screening millions of drug candidates, designing new proteins—this computational burden becomes prohibitive.

callout.html: Triangle attention is fast for small proteins but becomes prohibitively slow for large proteins or high-throughput screening.

steps.text: Start with a table of relationship values between all amino acid pairs.
Blend all pair signals together in one operation to mix each pair's influence through all others.
Optionally bias the result by sequence-level features for extra context.
Pass each updated pair value through a small neural network to compress/sharpen.
Stack 48 of these layers. Diffusion module then converts final pair values into 3D atoms.

object.h2: What changed: replace triangle attention with pair blending
paras: The paper removes triangle attention (expensive look-up) and replaces it with triangle multiplication (fast blending operation). Both operate on the same pair representation (the table of amino acid relationship values), but the computation is fundamentally different: attention requires comparing every pair separately, while multiplication blends all pairs at once.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: computational cost per layer
hidden.name: Attention operations per layer
paras: Triangle attention's cost grows with the number of amino acids. For each row in the pair table, it runs a full attention operation (comparing each position to all others). That is many separate lookups per layer. Triangle multiplication, by contrast, performs one blending operation regardless of how many amino acids there are.

The paper does not explicitly report a computational cost score, but it measures the proxy via training time (GPU-days on the RCSB dataset) and inference time (milliseconds on long sequences). Faster runtime shows fewer separate lookups per forward pass, because one blend step replaces many attention steps.

heat.caption: Darker means more lookups per layer. Triangle attention (left) scales with sequence length; triangle multiplication (right) is flat.

reads.html: Computational cost is how many separate steps the model must do. More steps means longer waiting.
Triangle attention runs comparisons for each row of the pair representation, producing many separate updates per layer; triangle multiplication produces the same refinement via one blended operation.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: blending preserves pairwise reasoning
paras: Both triangle attention and triangle multiplication are ways to mix information across the pair representation. Triangle attention explicitly looks at each pair and asks: which other pairs matter most? Triangle multiplication implicitly answers this by blending all pairs together at once: each output pair is a weighted blend of all input pairs (the weights are learned by training). The blended result carries the same relevant information, just computed differently.

Why the swap works: the diffusion module (the part that turns pair values into 3D atoms) does not care how the pair values were computed, only that they are accurate. Blending produces equally accurate pair values, just faster. The model can still express fine-grained constraints between amino acid triplets, because blending can learn any linear combination of input pairs (enough to encode spatial relationships).

Why it is faster: attention requires many individual lookups (one for each amino acid, for each pair, per layer), and each lookup itself is a comparison step. Blending does all that mixing in one fast operation on modern hardware, because processors are built to do a single pass over data quickly. Many separate lookups stall the processor; one blend keeps it busy doing useful work throughout.

stages.s: Pass each blended value through a small neural network
Refined pair representation with clearer signals

math.h2: The equation: triangle multiplication as a blending operation
math.words: For each layer, the pair representation is updated by multiplying the pair matrix by itself and optionally adding a bias from sequence features, then passing each pair through a feed-forward network.
math.equation: z_new = FFN(z @ z.T + alpha * s @ s.T)
symbols: the pair representation (L rows, L columns, C values per cell)
matrix multiply: pair times pair transpose
sequence feature vector (L elements, one per amino acid)
feed-forward network applied to each updated pair value

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Result: [[14, ?, ?], [12, ?, ?], [11, ?, ?]] (simplified). Each cell now mixes all pairs through the matrix multiply. Then FFN sharpens each value.

math.note: Matrix multiplication is faster than attention because modern hardware optimizes it as one bulk operation, whereas attention requires L separate comparisons.

charts.title: Pairformer (triangle attention)
charts.note: Standard AlphaFold backbone with expensive triangle attention. Accuracy is high, but computational cost is steep.

charts.title: Pairmixer (triangle multiplication)
charts.note: Pairmixer with blending. Trains 34% faster because fewer separate operations run per batch. Inference is 4x faster on long sequences because blending does not scale up with length, but many lookups do. Accuracy stays the same or improves, because blending preserves the model's ability to learn spatial relationships between amino acids.

items.b: Sequence bias is optional but fragile.
items.html: If the alpha (sequence bias strength) is set too high, the model over-trusts sequence similarity and misses spatial constraints encoded only in pairs.

items.b: Triple interactions are implicit, not explicit.
items.html: Blending mixes pairs globally, but the original triangle attention was designed to reason explicitly over triples (amino acid triplets). If a benchmark requires fine-grained triple reasoning, Pairmixer might underperform.

items.b: Other parts of the model still use attention.
items.html: Pairmixer only replaces the backbone layer; other parts (which convert pairs to 3D atoms) still use expensive lookups. Speed gains come only from the backbone.

Pairmixer works well when pair reasoning is sufficient (most structure prediction tasks). Train carefully on each domain (AlphaFold databases, ligand docking, de novo design) to tune alpha and layer counts for your task.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small protein-folding pipeline with both Pairformer and Pairmixer backbones. Train them on a subset of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) for the same number of GPU hours. Measure (1) training time per batch, (2) inference time per sequence, (3) final accuracy (mean LDDT score on a held-out test set).
demo.metric_eq: speedup = (Pairformer_inference_time - Pairmixer_inference_time) / Pairmixer_inference_time; accuracy_gap = Pairformer_LDDT - Pairmixer_LDDT
demo.closing: The demo proves blending is worth using if it cuts inference time in half on long sequences (400+ amino acids) while keeping accuracy within 1 point of the baseline, or improving it.
